summary: Design-science paper proposing the Agent Governance Manifest (AGM): a repository-hosted, machine-readable file of risk zones, evidence obligations, contributor-confirmation states and maintainer review gates for agent-mediated open-source contributions. An audit of 50 purposively sampled GitHub repositories (June 2026 snapshot) finds 58% have an agent instruction file but none has a project-wide arrangement that coordinates risk, evidence, accountability and gates. A within-subject study (15 participants using their own agent tools, 5 author-built tasks, 75 outputs) reports exact risk-label recovery of 37/38 with AGM materials vs 15/37 without, but the AGM condition hands reviewers the risk-zone rules, risk summaries and explicit gate states that the ordinary condition lacks.

claims.claim: No audited repository has a project-wide governability arrangement; 58% have an agent instruction file; only 4% have evidence-obligation cues
claims.evidence: Fig. 3 and §6.1-6.3; second coder on a stratified 15-repo subset agreed fully on artifact presence but produced 68 disagreements on the AI-governance construct, which the authors resolved by redefining the construct (§5.3, S2). 'None qualifies' is measured against the authors' own four-function criterion, which is essentially the AGM design, so the gap partly follows from the definition. Purposive sample, no prevalence claim.

claims.claim: AGM-supported materials improve exact risk-label recovery (37/38 vs 15/37; +56.8 pp, 95% CI 42.1-71.8)
claims.evidence: §7.2 and Table S30: the AGM condition provides 'risk-zone rules and risk summaries' and gate state 'as pass, needs-evidence, or blocked'; the ordinary condition has risk-zone reference 'not structured' and no gate state. The outcome therefore largely measures whether the label was present in the materials. Ordinary materials were sufficient on the low-risk task (T1). Participant-clustered bootstrap CIs and a 20-output second-coder check (full agreement on risk labels) are sound, but they quantify a near-circular comparison.

claims.claim: Perceived review support rises from 3.27 to 6.14 on a 1-7 scale
claims.evidence: §7.3: all 15 participants rated AGM higher; participants could not be blinded to an obviously richer condition and the questionnaire items (risk visibility, evidence sufficiency) mirror what AGM adds.

claims.claim: Contributor-side agents can prepare AGM evidence packages that preserve the contributor/maintainer boundary
claims.evidence: §7.5 and S7: separate cohort of 15, 45 tasks; 45/45 final packages had correct core governance state and 41/45 passed strict schema validation; no draft-to-final change altered risk labels. No comparison condition; tasks and validator are the authors'; one participant's interrupted run was replaced by a rerun. Feasibility only.

patterns.note: Audit: 29/50 repos (58%) have an agent instruction file (40% AGENTS.md, 30% CLAUDE.md, 20% Copilot instructions); coding finds they encode build/test/convention guidance rather than review or risk rules (§6.3). Descriptive only, no outcome measured.

AGM is machine-readable project context (risk zones by path, evidence schema, gate states) read by contributor and reviewer agents. The comparison is against materials that lack the same information, not against the same rules written as prose (CONTRIBUTING.md, PR template), so the effect of the machine-readable format is not isolated.

Explicit contributor-confirmation and maintainer-review states; the validator stops the contributor side from marking maintainer review complete. 45/45 packages respected the boundary, but there is no comparison condition. Observation: some agents skipped the pause-for-confirmation step unless the workflow prompted it (§7.5).
Governance rules as repository data plus validation scripts (policy-as-code for contributions); no comparison against CODEOWNERS or branch-protection alone.
AI provenance markers in 8.4% of 23,237 PRs; one repo (ClickHouse, 68.8% of its PRs) dominates; excluding it gives 7.0% (§6.4). Provenance treated as a lower bound.

methodology.sample: 50 purposively sampled GitHub repos (23,237 PRs, 19,884 issues); reviewer study 15 participants x 5 tasks = 75 outputs (38 AGM, 37 ordinary); contributor study 15 different participants x 3 tasks = 45
methodology.baselines: 'Ordinary materials' (task description, diff, PR description, test output) that omit the project's risk-zone definitions and gate state; no equal-information prose baseline; contributor study has no baseline
methodology.models: Participants' own agent tools (5 Codex, 6 Kilo Code variants, 2 OpenCode, 2 Continue variants); underlying models neither controlled nor reported
methodology.variance: Participant-clustered percentile bootstrap (10,000 resamples) for differences and ratios; second coder on 20 outputs (kappa 0.825-0.848 on evidence fields, full agreement on risk labels)
methodology.ablations: None; component-level evaluation (risk summary vs evidence index vs review packet) listed as future work
methodology.contamination_controls: n/a; tasks author-built; condition allocation alternated and task order cyclically rotated
methodology.languages: Not language-specific; tasks cover documentation, test/config, core logic, authentication and CI-workflow changes

standards.artifacts: AGM prototype repository and v0.1 specification public; replication package 'will be made available' and excludes participant task materials, outputs, free-text responses and prompts
standards.preregistration: Allocation described as pre-specified; no registry cited

biases.detail: Exact risk-label recovery in the AGM arm mostly measures reading a label that the AGM materials supply (Table S30); it does not show that AGM improves judgement on changes whose risk is not pre-stated.
The ordinary arm lacks the project's risk-zone rules entirely; the realistic alternative (same rules in prose docs or a PR template) is not tested.
Authors designed the artifact, the tasks, the reference labels, the rubric and coded the outputs.
15 participants per study and 5 reviewer tasks; the risk-label effect is concentrated in 4 tasks.
Convenience pool of students, teachers, professionals and one OSS organisation member; all frequent AI-tool users; not maintainers of real projects.

Contribution policy, PR templates, CODEOWNERS-style risk zones and review checklists are reframed as 'governability infrastructure' and 'governable boundary objects'; heavy theory relative to the mechanism.

coi.affiliations: Shanxi University of Finance and Economics; North University of China; University of Warwick
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: None commercial; AGM is the authors' own open specification
coi.detail: No vendor interest. Authors evaluate their own artifact on their own tasks (recorded as self_evaluation).

verdict_reason: The 50-repo audit is a usable descriptive data point on what instruction files contain and what they lack. The headline experiment is close to circular: reviewers recover risk labels and gate states that the treatment materials state outright, against a baseline missing that information. The contributor-side check shows feasibility, not benefit.
applicability: Little direct transfer to the discovery and onboarding harness: AGM targets review-time governance of outside contributions, not knowledge gathering before the spec. The idea worth taking is a single repo-hosted, machine-readable map from paths to risk zones and required evidence, read by both the agent preparing a change and the human reviewer. For a 4-repo Java ingestion team, such a map (for example PHI-adjacent code, content-validation rules, delivery API contracts) is one way to put tacit 'this area is dangerous' knowledge in front of new developers and their agents. This paper only shows that people find a label when it is written down. It does not show that the format beats prose, or that review workload drops, so measure on real PRs. The contributor-side observation that agents skip confirmation pauses unless the workflow forces them supports putting confirmation steps in deterministic hooks rather than in agent instructions.
